VpnHoodWindowsApp and VpnHoodLinuxApp take their paths as one object, VpnHoodWindowsAppPaths and VpnHoodLinuxAppPaths, instead of a row of strings that could be passed in each other's place: the storage, the single-instance lock's folder (Windows: null for the service's own lock; Linux: required) and, on Linux, the kill switch's way-out script. The daemon hosts take the same object; the factories and MAUI's Windows host name each path Tested: the Windows and Linux heads and MAUI's Windows host build; VpnHood.AppLib.Test.

Kill switch, forwarded traffic (the desktop plan's test 8): on Linux the forward chain now blocks DNS as the output chain does, an out-of-tunnel plan's resolvers excepted - a container's query to the LAN's router left eth0 while the host's own got EPERM. On Windows, WinNAT's traffic - WSL2's NAT mode, so Docker Desktop's too - is a known limit (owner, 2026-11-01), now said in WindowsVpnKillSwitch's comment, which claimed WSL2, Hyper-V's switches and Docker were covered: no WFP layer sees it, so it goes into the tunnel while one is up and around the block while none is; the forward layers cover Windows' own routing, and have no port field to block DNS by Tested: Docker on the Ubuntu 26.04 VM, the default bridge and a network of its own - connected, a container's traffic and names go through the tunnel and its LAN DNS no longer leaves eth0; the service killed and its restart held, a container's internet TCP is refused, its DNS dropped, the LAN split passes. WSL2 3.0.3 on the Windows Server 2025 Desktop VM with nested virtualization - connected, through the tunnel; the service killed, straight to the internet; a block for one address at the forward, IP packet, transport, connect and vSwitch layers stopped Windows' own connection at three of them and WSL's at none; Windows' own routing (the Ubuntu VM routed through it) blocked, and through once lifted.
